title: DDIM likelihood not evaluated
description: The authors did not attempt to calculate negative log-likelihood using DDIM sampling because DDIM does not present a simple way of estimating likelihood.
canonical_description: Likelihood evaluation not performed for alternative fast sampling method

evidence.anchor: We did not attempt to calculate NLL using DDIM
evidence.quote: We did not attempt to calculate NLL using DDIM, since [CITE:ddim] does not present NLL results or a simple way of estimating likelihood under DDIM.

verdict.reasoning: Both assessments are "not_addressed." Paper 1 (Path Integral) develops likelihood evaluation for stochastic sampling processes, not for DDIM; it explicitly notes that deterministic ODE-based samplers like DDIM already have a known likelihood method via change-of-variables, but it does not actually compute or report DDIM likelihood. Paper 2 (OGDM) improves sample quality under fast sampling but reports only FID and recall, never computing or reporting negative log-likelihood (bits/dim) for DDIM or any other method. The original gap — that DDIM likelihood was not evaluated because no simple method was known — remains completely unaddressed by both papers.

paper.title: Understanding Diffusion Models by Feynman's Path Integral
paper.abstract: Score-based diffusion models have proven effective in image generation and have gained widespread usage; however, the underlying factors contributing to the performance disparity between stochastic and deterministic (i.e., the probability flow ODEs) sampling schemes remain unclear. We introduce a novel formulation of diffusion models using Feynman's path integral, which is a formulation originally developed for quantum physics. We find this formulation providing comprehensive descriptions of score-based generative models, and demonstrate the derivation of backward stochastic differential equations and loss functions.The formulation accommodates an interpolating parameter connecting stochastic and deterministic sampling schemes, and we identify this parameter as a counterpart of Planck's constant in quantum physics. This analogy enables us to apply the Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) expansion, a well-established technique in quantum physics, for evaluating the negative log-likelihood to assess the performance disparity between stochastic and deterministic sampling schemes.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper develops a path integral formulation of diffusion models and uses WKB expansion to compute negative log-likelihood for stochastic sampling processes (where noise is present in generation). It introduces an interpolating parameter $\mathfrak{h}$ connecting stochastic ($\mathfrak{h}=1$) and deterministic/ODE ($\mathfrak{h}=0$) sampling, and provides a perturbative expansion in $\mathfrak{h}$ to compute NLL corrections. The paper explicitly acknowledges that for deterministic ODE-based samplers ($\mathfrak{h}=0$), likelihood can already be computed via the standard change-of-variables formula.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is about DDIM (a deterministic fast sampling method) not having a simple way to estimate likelihood. However, the paper itself notes that deterministic ODE-based samplers like DDIM already have a well-known method for likelihood evaluation via the change-of-variables formula (instantaneous change-of-variables for ODE flows). The paper does not address DDIM at all — it addresses the separate problem of evaluating likelihood for stochastic sampling processes, which is a different issue. The specific gap of "DDIM likelihood not evaluated" remains unaddressed because (a) the paper doesn't mention DDIM, and (b) the paper's contribution is about stochastic sampling likelihood, while DDIM is a deterministic sampler where likelihood evaluation is already possible via existing methods.
evidence_snippets: In deterministic sampling schemes based on ODEs, one can directly calculate log-likelihood based on the change-of-variables formula [CITE:chen2018neural] [CITE:song2020score] [CITE:lipman2022flow].

Within stochastic sampling processes in contrast to deterministic ones, a direct evaluation method of the NLL remains elusive, though a theoretical bound exists for the NLL [CITE:kong2023information].
To our best knowledge, there is no stochastic case where the values of log-likelihood have ever been calculated.

paper.title: Observation-Guided Diffusion Probabilistic Models
paper.abstract: We propose a novel diffusion-based image generation method called the observation-guided diffusion probabilistic model (OGDM), which effectively addresses the tradeoff between quality control and fast sampling. Our approach reestablishes the training objective by integrating the guidance of the observation process with the Markov chain in a principled way. This is achieved by introducing an additional loss term derived from the observation based on a conditional discriminator on noise level, which employs a Bernoulli distribution indicating whether its input lies on the (noisy) real manifold or not. This strategy allows us to optimize the more accurate negative log-likelihood induced in the inference stage especially when the number of function evaluations is limited. The proposed training scheme is also advantageous even when incorporated only into the fine-tuning process, and it is compatible with various fast inference strategies since our method yields better denoising networks using the exactly the same inference procedure without incurring extra computational cost. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our training algorithm using diverse inference techniques on strong diffusion model baselines. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/Junoh-Kang/OGDM_edm.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes OGDM, a training method that adds a discriminator-based observation loss to diffusion model training to improve sample quality under fast sampling. It derives theoretical connections to negative log-likelihood surrogates and shows improved FID/recall scores with few-step samplers (Euler, Heun, PNDM) on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and LSUN Church. However, it does not compute or report negative log-likelihood values for any sampling method, including DDIM.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is specifically about the lack of likelihood evaluation for DDIM sampling. This paper does not compute, report, or evaluate negative log-likelihood (bits/dim) for DDIM or any other fast sampling method. It only reports FID and recall. The theoretical analysis discusses NLL bounds but no actual likelihood numbers are provided. The original gap — that DDIM does not present a simple way of estimating likelihood and therefore likelihood was not evaluated — remains completely unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: We measure FID~[CITE:heusel2017gans] and recall~[CITE:kynkaanniemi2019improved] using the implementation provided by ADM\footref{fn:adm} for quantitative evaluation.

While we examine the observations following the Bernoulli distribution and implement them using the discriminators as in GANs, it is important to note that there are other options to define and implement the observation factors.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The gap is quite tractable: (1) A known method already exists — the probability flow ODE (Song et al. 2021) provides an instantaneous change-of-variables formula for likelihood evaluation, and DDIM is a discretization of this ODE, so the mathematical foundation is mature. (2) No new model training is needed; any pretrained DDPM can be evaluated. (3) Compute is modest — trace estimation via Hutchinson's trick requires O(d) forward passes per sample, feasible on a single GPU for CIFAR-10 or ImageNet 32x32. (4) The scope is sharply defined: report bits/dim for DDIM sampling at various step counts. (5) Evaluation is clear (negative log-likelihood, comparable to existing DDPM/score-SDE numbers). The only moderate difficulty is that ODE-based likelihood depends on integration accuracy (step count, solver choice), and DDIM's specific discretization may not perfectly match the continuous ODE likelihood, requiring some careful numerical work. Overall, this is an empirical benchmarking task, not a fundamental breakthrough.
